caption:
Why did the South Sea Bubble burst? And how did Isaac Newton lose money in it?

The South Sea Company was founded in 1711 to swallow Britain's national debt. In exchange it got a monopoly on trade with South America — territory Spain controlled, and Britain was at war with Spain. There was no realistic prospect of trade, and the company never made significant profit from the monopoly.

The income it did have came from trafficking enslaved Africans under the Asiento granted in 1713. The company trafficked more than 34,000 people; about 4,000 died on the Middle Passage. Even that was unprofitable — the real money came from contraband smuggled in the slave ships.

Shares went from about £100 in early 1720 to nearly £1,000 by August. Directors talked up the New World trade with "the most extravagant rumours". Politicians were handed shares they never paid for, with the right to sell them back at any price. John Blunt's idea to prop the price up: lend people money to buy the company's own shares.

By September the stock was at £150. Thousands were ruined. Parliament found the Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Aislabie, guilty of "most notorious, dangerous and infamous corruption" and imprisoned him. All 33 directors were stripped of, on average, 82% of their wealth.

Newton held nearly £22,000 of the stock in 1722 and lost at least £10,000. Asked whether it would keep rising, he said he could not calculate the madness of people.

Still unresolved: that quotation reaches us secondhand, reported by Joseph Spence from Lord Radnor, and survives in more than one wording.

Images: Hogarth's "The South Sea Scheme"; a 1720 Bubble Card; a £1,000 share certificate of 22 June 1720; Thomas Bowles's engraving of South Sea House, 1754; Rowlandson and Pugin's Dividend Hall, 1810; Herman Moll's map of the Company's limits, 1711.
